utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Morrison being away due to his official engagement. Good morning, General. Good morning, Mr. Karadzic. You have two hours today to conclude your cross-examination. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Chamber should perhaps be aware of the following - you mentioned this - unfortunately, General Simic passed away two days ago. Could we now see 1D5302. Not Simatovic. His name is Novica Simic. I don't think, I have the Serbian translation at this point in time, or, rather, the Serbian original, but, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you check. Do you follow the proceedings? Do you hear me, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Wasn't General Simic on the list of our witnesses -- or Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning. Good morning, General. He was indeed, Your Honours. We knew that, unfortunately, he was ill, but we -- I didn't have that information before, but, yes, he was on the witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember this protest of yours that you lodged on the 30th of March, 1993, because -- I'll read it out in the English: [In English] "We strongly protest because of open units of the humanitarian convoy escort troops and Muslim forces. "Four days ago, in area of village Pelemis, English APC opened fire with four rounds of anti-tank rockets to our forces and destroyed one tank and one AAA vehicle 'Praga'." "We hope that you are aware in the fact that Muslim in Tuzla paint their army and civilian vehicles in white, and they put UN signs on them. With UN signs ... arms they fire to our forces in the area the Kladanj and Olovo. "We expect and demand your efficient steps against responsible persons in English battalion and against every other abuse of UN signs. On that way, you will improve safety of UNPROFOR forces and humanitarian convoy escort forces on field. Your passive attitude may contribute to unwanted consequences." [Interpretation] Could the interpreters read the text from the screen. Do you remember, this General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was document that was sent to General Valgren, the commander of the UNPROFOR forces for the former Yugoslavia. You can see that it was sent four days after the event. During the previous four days, I contacted the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR over the phone. He was the commander of UNPROFOR at the time for Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, they did not react and I thought it would be appropriate for me to contact the commander of UNPROFOR for the former Yugoslavia. I don't remember his reaction or his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Am I correct if I said that you reacted in writing and over the phone only when there were more serious violations or, rather, incidents, only when there was a notable bias towards our enemies and other incidents, incidents that we did not react to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have a look at 1D05318.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at this order of yours that is based on the report according to which humanitarian organisations are being used to deliver fuel to the enclaves to be used for military needs, and you didn't stop the convoys, but you requested that the fuel be checked. Have a look at paragraph number 1 and paragraph number 5 and tell us -- or tell me what are the reasons for these measures of precaution.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On Thursday, on the last day, I also spoke about the fact that we obtained information according to which fuel from the tanks was being delivered to the enclaves and fuel as well as ammunition and weapons. Food and clothes are considered strategic equipment. So I don't know whom they were delivering this to in the enclaves, but I had the right to suspect them of delivering these things to the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2170, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we remember the telegram from Thursday in which Oric said, As soon as the food arrives, we'll take Bratunac, here we can see as soon as the fuel comes, we saw that the international forces pretended that they had training and that's how they justified the delivery of ammunition. So does this justify the suspicions we had with regard to the international community providing our enemies with assistance?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see 1D5338. And while waiting for that, General, do you agree that we noticed that as a rule every time a convoy would enter the demilitarised zones the Muslim forces were a lot more combative and the attacks they launched would be more fierce?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say given the time that has passed, but I do know that they continued attacking us from the enclaves and UNPROFOR was aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a look at this. This is a document of yours sent to the command of the Sarajevo Romanija and Drina Corps dated the 8th of November, 1994. And you say that UNPROFOR wants to deliver certain goods in containers and often they don't say what the containers contain, and so on and so forth, and your order is that each request should be examined, and if quantities of goods have not been specified, you should reject them. There were cases of abuse when in the lower part of the container there was a lot of ammunition, weapons, and other prohibited items. Do you remember this? Was this also a reason for our concern with regard to the free passage of convoys?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This can't be a document of mine. I was at Plitvice at a meeting with Martic on that day and with Fikret Abdic. A deputy of mine must have drafted this because the document hasn't been signed. Someone should have probably put "for" at the bottom, General Miletic or someone who was replacing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. This number 09, 09, does this show that it was some kind of a forward command post, the protocol number at the top.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 09, it's the personnel administration of the Main Staff. The duty officer in the command of the Main Staff was probably someone from that administration, and he's the person who drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but the document is an authentic one. You have no doubts about that. It's being sent to Bresa, Domar, Caura.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it saves time, I'm not challenging the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could it be admitted? And did someone from the staff who drafted it, that should be noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's admit it as Exhibit D2171.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D5324, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the second day after Christmas. It's dated the 8th of January, 1994. I'm writing to you about the decision of the Main Staff. It's following a decision of mine the Main Staff has to establish a single system for the delivery of humanitarian aid. Since in the meantime there has been certain disagreement between some organs regarding the implementation of this decision, we reiterate that this decision remains in force, and so on and so forth. Have a look at the next at the last paragraph. We point out that if you don't respect this decision and act wilfully, you will act to the detriment of the reputation of Republika Srpska, and so on and so forth. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this one dated as this one is, but we received various warnings of the same or similar kind, various warnings in writing, over the phone, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I agree -- would you agree that some of my warnings, some of my criticism, wasn't justified because I believed foreign elements, and often they were not right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I just wonder if we could have some foundation or basis for how the general is meant to answer the question of what Mr. Karadzic's motivation was at the time, and -- I don't have the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's the part I objected to is "... because I believed foreign elements." How does the witness know what Mr. Karadzic believed unless there's some basis given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, could you answer the question as far as in the capacity as the recipient of this letter, or would you like Mr. Karadzic to reformulate his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that given the principle of the chain of command, it's not for me to assess whether documents that come from the supreme commander are justified or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And can I put the question in this way: When I trusted foreign agencies and this wasn't justified, wasn't the result that there was some tension between the civilian and military structures, because I took their criticism to be justified, but that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already spoken about this in the course of my testimony here. You often accepted information from people who weren't responsible for such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have a look at 1D5346.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the order by General Zivanovic seven days following directive 7. He ordered all subordinate brigades to treat humanely the members of UNPROFOR. He mentions numerous complaints, which is in the third line when he refers to the peacekeeping mission, and further down he says there have been cases of robbery against UNPROFOR personnel before, but such cases have become ever-more frequent in recent months. It has happened that groups of armed and uniformed persons stop UNPROFOR vehicles. Then he goes on to say that it has also happened that some UNPROFOR personnel have been physically abused as have citizens of Republika Srpska who, at that moment, were in contact with UNPROFOR personnel at the Mostar junction on the Sarajevo-Kiseljak road. A group of armed persons disarmed the UNPROFOR officers, et cetera, et cetera. Such acts have inexplicably become manifestations of patriotism and heroism. He further goes on to say that he orders all the commands to engage all available forces to undertake investigative measures as needed. Can we change the page in the Serbian. The goal is to have the perpetrators of these grave crimes found and prosecuted, and the property should be returned to UNPROFOR. General, was this order by Zivanovic in keeping with the policy of the VRS concerning UNPROFOR, irrespective of our complaints as to the conduct of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because you asked the question, you put -- because you put like this: This order was issued seven days following the directive 7. So you are telling us that directive 7 was issued or notified to the Drina Corps seven days before this order. Is it your case, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think he was notified, but it seems that this was the prevailing feeling in the VRS and that nothing much has changed in our position vis-a-vis UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps general could clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was issued six days following the publication of directive 7 and has nothing to do with its contents. This was a result of a process which developed in the VRS to the effect that our personnel stole vehicles from UNPROFOR, and not only vehicles; for example, I had an unpleasant incident, was at a meeting with General Hayes upon his arrival in Bosnia. We met in Sokolac, and he presented me with a bullet-proof vest. But when we were about to go our own ways, he returned from his car and he said, General, someone broke into my car and stole things from the car. My bullet-proof vest was also stolen. We managed to find the perpetrator. It was one of the drivers from Pale. So such occurrences began taking place. This was General Zivanovic's reaction. I couldn't see what he referred to in the order specifically, but he wasn't referring to directive number 7. We were simply trying to put a stop to such conduct in the VRS. Perhaps I can also add this: UNPROFOR applied certain measures. For example, I was stopped in Brod, near Foca, and they scratched my vehicle with a nail. They were basically trying to scrape the top layer of paint to see whether there's white paint underneath and to determine whether this had been their vehicle that was stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for your explanation. Can we agree that such incidents did not enjoy the support of command structures and that efforts were made to put a stop to it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that they did not enjoy the support, but quite could the contrary. Such incidents were sanctioned. People were disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we not admit it? It was to be admitted 2173.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D5427.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you recall that UNPROFOR was present in our country with our approval, which we provided concerning their initial mandate which was not supposed to be changed without our agreement? And since you haven't begun your answer yet, that mandate completely excluded any possibility of their taking sides or engaging in combat against any of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The other day I did not explain to you the third mandate of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina which had to do with the protection of protected areas. However, they assigned a fourth mandate to themselves, although I had never seen a Security Council Resolution as to that. They basically began -- became involved in the conflicts or clashes between the warring sides. They simply took upon themselves to determine who was to blame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember this document of November 23rd? After NATO air-strikes which were guided from the ground, as well as your reaction to any -- to the phone calls made by UNPROFOR commanders from the field, as a result of that you ordered a change of disposition towards UNPROFOR, because they became enemy with everything that entailed. Was this a legitimate position to take?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is true I ordered this without having consulted the Main Staff or you since General Rose acted inhumanely and less than chivalrously. He struck at me, at my forces, because I approached the non-existing delineation of the protected area of Bihac. I need to say, and I believe I mentioned that in my book, that the borders of the security area of Bihac were received by my office one day following this order, that is to say on November 24th, which is one and a half year following the establishment or formation of the protected area borders around Bihac. The line went along the positions of my forces. According to such borders as they were delineated, he had no reason to attack my forces, whereas, as a matter of fact, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that such borders could only be set by the joint commission of the warring sides, and once an agreement is reached to that effect, any combat or fighting activity from the area needs to cease?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I discussed it the other day. The Security Council, after the commanders of the warring sides signed an agreement for Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, unilaterally declared Tuzla, Sarajevo, and Bihac protect areas without setting borders, and it did not mandate UNPROFOR with disarming the Muslim forces in the area. So in Tuzla, the 2nd Muslim Corps was in full function with its staff units, and that corps pulled out front brigades and located them in Tuzla for periods of rest, which is considered a combat activity. Next, in Sarajevo their Supreme Command was in function, the Muslim forces command, as well as the 1st Muslim Corps, which was 50 to 70 armed men -- 70.000 armed men strong. In Bihac, the 5th Muslim Corps grew in size. On the day this Resolution was put in place about Bihac as a safe area, it numbered three brigades, and under this regimen it increased to the size of a corps of 22.000 soldiers who were equipped with the latest equipment as -- and, as such, was one of the most modern units in Europe at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2174, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 1D5332.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you agree with this position of mine: Aiding and rooting for the Muslim side was a bad call to make because it provided for a continuation of the war which could not be resolved by any other means than a conference?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether it was a bad call to make is something I cannot say, but they were definitely doing them a favour, and by having done so, UNPROFOR consciously extended the war. And I have explained that when I discussed Mount Igman and Bjelasnica which, to me, were the most unbelievable areas to be proclaimed safe areas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this document, General? We see your signature at the bottom. There you inform, on top of other things, that the bombing of Serbian positions at Gorazde was greeted with anger, and that you had to take measures to pacify the soldiers and to prevent them from taking revenge not only against UNPROFOR but foreigners as well, and you informed the Main Staff about this from a forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was my forward command post near Brcko at Kosa Vranovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2175, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D5331.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, let's have a look at how long our anger lasted. On the 19th of April, you say that based on the order of the president, you imposed the status quo ante, which means the situation as it had been before the enemy activities by NATO and UNPROFOR were taken. You order that things should continue as they had before we broke any relations -- we broke off any relations with them.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that; however, we broke relations with UNPROFOR also pursuant to your order, although I don't remember whether it was an oral or written one. It was at the time when General Mladic was away, because he attended his daughter's funeral and was allowed to take a leave for some 40 days. It was following our operation Zvezda 94. At first, you ordered that we cease all contact and relations, and some eight days following that initial order, you backtracked, it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems that Mr. Akashi, was very persuading so I gave up on my position. Do you recall in any case that General Mladic said that close support is received by UNPROFOR when engaging our forces and that we could engage them freely whenever it happened and that we never approved to any such guided air attacks with close support?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question who was to engage whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify. General Mladic, and it's in the various minutes of UNPROFOR, told them that if our soldiers attack you, you are hereby authorised by me to engage them. No one has the right to attack you. This is something referred to as close-air support. If they are in danger, they are entitled to defence. However, their expansion of mandates to include air-strikes, which had nothing to do with support provided to them but were aimed at changing the situation in the theatre of war, was an enemy act. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the last part of your question, which is also a conclusion. Physically threatening UNPROFOR -- VRS soldiers, physically threatening UNPROFOR, or UNPROFOR threatening VRS soldiers, and that was a case that you could read about in my letter to Valgren, well, it really wasn't even necessary to warn about such things. It's part of the code of conduct for armed individuals. Armed individuals have to defend themselves if they are attacked. So I cannot confirm or deny that statement of General Mladic's at some meeting because I wasn't usually present at those meetings when Mladic was there, nor was he present at meetings when I was leading a delegation. So as to whether he said that or not, I cannot say. I can't confirm that, nor can I deny it, but I do know that there was such a position in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us whether it's logical and justified if someone acts like an enemy and is armed, that person is then considered to be an enemy, and in April 1994 did UNPROFOR in a one-week period -- well, was UNPROFOR treated as an enemy during that period, and capturing them was a matter of capturing prisoners of war. It wasn't a matter of taking hostages.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your order after the 11th of April, after the first bombing, in fact -- I've already spoken about this, but on that occasion you broke off the relationship between the VRS and UNPROFOR, as you considered UNPROFOR to be the enemy regardless of this order of yours dated the 19th when you re-established contact, well, I can say that I never did this. UNPROFOR received the approval of the Security Council, the authorisation to engage NATO forces when the UNPROFOR commander believed that this was appropriate and necessary. So from my personal point of view, and this was in the case of the supreme commander in the Main Staff, for me from that day until the end of the war, up until the 14th of September, 1995, in fact, I considered UNPROFOR to be the enemy. Because in spite of the fact that they hadn't declared war on the -- on Republika Srpska, they were one of the warring factions. I'm afraid I haven't understood what the purpose of your question was, but it's not for me to put questions to you, so that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd just like to intervene for the sake of the transcript. You said even if that was not the case with the Supreme Command and the Main Staff, the Main Staff and the Supreme Command did not consider them to be the enemy, but you, nevertheless, personally considered them to be the enemy; isn't that correct? So that opinion differs from the opinion or the position of the Main Staff and the Supreme Command. That was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a difference between the Supreme Command and the Main Staff on the ones hand and myself on the other hand. You no longer believed that UNPROFOR was our enemy, but my personal conviction was that they were still the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5334, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this letter of yours that you sent to me -- or, rather, to the Supreme Command but addressed to me, where you protest because we easily agree to the presence of UNPROFOR soldiers. It's the 3rd of May, immediately after this crisis. We accept their presence at our lines where we are not in a good strategic or tactical position, and in the last -- or the penultimate paragraph you say you're surprised that the Main Staff hasn't been consulted and you ask me to take your opinion into consideration before taking a final decision. Do you remember that I acted in this way, and I believe that they didn't go there in the manner that they wanted to deploy there? They weren't able to do exactly what they thought they were going to do.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I personally intervened, personally contacted you on a number of occasions because I had information -- or, rather, proof from the field to the effect that the UNPROFOR intelligence was working for its own needs and for the Muslim army. They were providing information on us to them, but they never provided us with any information about the Muslims. I always wanted to warn you not to trust UNPROFOR with regard to everything, because in these places, in these bottleneck places, there was the increased level of threat for the VRS. And I did contact you on one occasion because when politicians are negotiating with the enemy, with the warring faction, and generals attend those negotiations, or should attend those negotiations, because the politicians dilute the essence of combat activities. They make concession and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2177, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D5345.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for that, General, I'll show you two Muslim documents which confirm that they are receiving intelligence on our positions, intelligence from UNPROFOR. I don't know where the Serbian version is, but this is also a document of yours dated the 2nd of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I be assisted in finding the Serbian version. Could it be found anywhere? If not, I'll read this part in the box which says the following: "Information on the enemy offensive carried out"--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can print a copy, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You found the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in this paragraph, you state that the enemy received accurate information on our forces and their deployment, and so on and so forth. And when carrying out this attack, the enemy used the element of surprise by attacking Vlasic, Srbobran, and it says they had very detailed information. Please have a look at this information on the enemy offensive carried out against Mount Vlasic on the 24th and 25th of February. It's the first paragraph. And then we'll have a look at something else. When you've read through that passage, have a look at the conclusion. It's the third page in the English version, "Conclusion and moral." Here you say that although they had prepared everything, they weren't successful when launching that offensive. Our forces reorganised themselves and managed to neutralise this element of surprise that was made possible by NATO and UNPROFOR. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember this document, but I'm not sure whether that is your only question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. I want to ask you whether this is confirmation of the information we had, information that UNPROFOR was acting as an intelligence service for our enemy. Is this also the act of an enemy?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is another confirmation of my personal conviction that UNPROFOR was our enemy. There's the saying the friend of my enemy is also my enemy; or the enemy of my enemy is my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, did you have some specific proof as to your information that the UNPROFOR was acting as an intelligence service, or did some of the UNPROFOR officials confirm such information at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I had proof. The interceptions of the VRS, there was information on our mutual conversations, and UNPROFOR would provide those intercepts to the Muslim army. The most obvious proof is this document that Mr. Karadzic has just shown. They knew exactly what our weakest points were thanks to the information that UNPROFOR provided them with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have look at two documents, or could we put two documents on the ELMO, in fact. They refer to this matter. We didn't upload them. I didn't think the -- this subject matter would be on the agenda. I'd just like to do this very briefly to deal with these two documents that comes from the Muslim side, and I would also request the other party for its indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you'd like, I can read it out aloud: "With regard to your request from your communications dispatch, we hereby inform you that in order to check our previously obtained information, we spoke to Colonel Roger from the British Battalion. In the course of the conversation, Roger confirmed ..." Could it be clearer?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Our information obtained from officer Allen was confirmed. He said that the regrouping of the aggressor was noticed. Three brigades were regrouping in the wider Trnovo sector. He said that we shouldn't be concerned by this because in his assessment it was a matter of 1.500 or 1.600 enemy soldiers. And then it refers to the situation in Srebrenica and so on and so forth. Chief of sector Midhat Senovic. So did we know, as a result of having intercepted their conversations -- well, here, two UNPROFOR officers are mentioned who provided information on the deployment our forces.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document's date is two days prior to the Muslim offensive, the purpose of which was to raise the blockade of Sarajevo, or, rather, to occupy Sarajevo. Those three brigades mentioned here were probably Serbian forces that were regrouping for a counter-offensive or for the defence of the Serbian part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe Mr. Reid was able to find a translation, if Mr. Karadzic would like to put it on the ELMO. I don't know. It's up to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we take a look briefly. Why don't we put it on the ELMO. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D2179, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the next document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of July it says: "We are hereby inform you that on the 1st of July, in the evening..." Oh, there's a translation of that as well, is there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection. If I can have the ERN number, we can check for -- to see if we have a translation, but I can't see the whole number at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you see -- could you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please show us the number at the top of the page. A bit more. A bit more. 543-84635, is it? Can we please see it? We cannot see it on the ELMO. It's the upper right-hand corner. Yes. Thank you. 8460.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Gordon Riley. They were invited for a brief get-together, and he is prepared to give us part of the information he obtained through a telephone conversation with General Smith. On this occasion, Colonel John said that Karadzic is terrorists with a view to discrediting their forces around Sarajevo within the next few days, and he did not know what the precise date would be, would carry out an attack in the territory of Sapna Kalesija. As the conversation continued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the B/C/S version to the General and put the English translation on the ELMO. Yes. Yes, we can read it. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, is this pre-eminent intelligence to the benefit of our enemy? Is this a hostile act?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2180, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please call up P2137. It's been admitted as a Prosecution document. I'm not sure that this is it. P -- or, actually, 65 ter 3656.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, could you please focus on this document, which is another document of yours from the time when our positions were massively bombed at the end of May 1995, and what is ordered here is the deployment of members of UNPROFOR. Could you please take a look at this document. Do you agree, General, that they had been taken prisoner, these members of UNPROFOR, and that they were treated as prisoners of war, and that is the status that they, themselves, invoked, and they enjoyed the rights of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I give a brief history of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please just look at page 2 and then --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, the second subparagraph: "During the transportation and reception of UNPROFOR staff, make sure that they are treated properly with military respect, treat them as prisoners of war and provide them with food and water, just like what the members of the Army of Republika Srpska have." And further down, it says: "The above-mentioned order of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska concerning the deployment of UNPROFOR staff has been approved by the President of Republika Srpska and local and foreign media were also informed about it." Tell us what is important in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after this comment of yours, nothing really matters any longer. I can just say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that it wasn't only troops on the ground that had ordered bombing? There were forward air controllers on the ground, and they led the gunners from the aircraft to our targets.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether members of UNPROFOR acted as forward air controllers bringing missiles to our targets, but I know that after the actual fire, members of UNPROFOR came to these positions to see what the effect of the fire were; that is to say that they joined in the campaign of bombing the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? I beg your pardon. This is actually already been admitted as a Prosecution document. 1D5343. Can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that during the bombing civilian bridges were also hit and that there were civilian casualties? In a small Fiat car some persons were killed.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't remember the individual case of the little Fiat and the bridge, but I know that in the Main Staff after these three days of bombing we analysed the effects, and we established then that about 110 civilians were killed. Most of them were shepherds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to ask you to take a look at this document dated the 30th of August, 1995. That is another document of yours, and may I remind you this is actually the beginning of the second massive bombing in that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we looking at the correct translation? It seems different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation is not the right one, no. The translation has a different date. The date of this document is the 30th of August, 1995. 1D5343 is the number of the document. It's the wrong translation. We've uploaded the wrong document under this number. So then can we remove the English page until we find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you remember this document when in the early morning hours this massive bombing started that led to the final decline in our combat capacity? You speak about the consequences here, and in paragraph 2, you say: "Due to the realistic threat of the enemy (NATO, UNPROFOR, and the Muslim-Croat coalition) will continue combat activities against the Army of Republika Srpska from the ground and from airspace. Take immediate measures for the entire manpower to be protected to a maximum degree from these attacks." Was it clear that this was a coalition - NATO, UNPROFOR, and the Muslim-Croat coalition - and that this meant co-ordinated action?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, this co-ordinated action started a bit before the 30th of August. It seems to me that often I write or speak in vain. The Croatian armed forces - on the 4th of June, 1995, at the same moment when I started a new counter-attack towards Bihac - carried out an aggression against the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Livanjsko Polje towards Glamoc and Grahovo. Fire support of the Croatian forces during those 110 days, while Operation Storm went on, was given to the Croats by the Rapid Deployment Corps. That was the name of the Euro corps. I was hit in that area from the broader area of Duvansko Polje - nowadays it's called Tomislavgrad - under the command of French General Sobiru [as interpreted]. And I thought that we were friends. Part of this corps attacked the Serb forces defending Sarajevo in that offensive of theirs from the 16th until the 25th of June under the command of American General Sylvester, who was the Chief of Staff of this Euro corps. This Euro corps consisted of French and Spanish troops. The commander was a Frenchman, which is only natural. However, the Chief of Staff was an American, Sylvester. A few years later this Sylvester came to Bosnia as a SFOR commander. Look at the book of Mr. Carl Bildt and you will see that what I'm saying is correct. I think that it's called "Peace Mission in Bosnia," whatever. It doesn't matter. So co-ordinated action of the forces of the European Community, the then-European community. This was a test corps for Europe to see whether they it could have its own armed forces. These activities that started on the 30th of August started a day earlier. There were reconnaissance flights and reconnaissance sorties, and this went on for 17 days. There were 17 days of bombing. This was pure air support to the Croatian forces; that is to say the forces of the regular army of Croatia and the forces of Alija Izetbegovic. To be more specific, his 5th and 7th Corps. Mr. Karadzic, I have to use part of your time to say this: There is this general misconception in the world and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is the Split declaration achieved between Alija Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman in the town of Split on the 22nd of July. There is this belief that this Split declaration led to Croatian Operation Storm, and the greatest misconception, and I spoke about that when I first testified here in this courtroom, was that Operation Storm was on on the 4th and 5th of August, when Knin and Petrinja fell. Storm started on the 4th of June, 1995, and it went on. Later on it was transformed into Operation Maestral, Breeze in order to have this area occupied, Visoko Krajina; that is to say including Kljuc and Petrovac. And then the third stage of that operation, Oluja, was Juzni Potez. That was the name of the operation. The Croats were rather successful and they wanted to take Banja Luka. You and I defended ourselves on the approaches to Banja Luka. I'm saying this because it is believed that Operation Storm started by the Split declaration, which is not correct. Tudjman deceived Izetbegovic by way of the Split declaration in order to have Izetbegovic allow the passage of Croatian forces through Bosnia and Herzegovina so that Tudjman would relieve the Croatian Army of the attribute of aggressor, which is indeed what it was because they had attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what I wished to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time. We'll sit till 1.45 today. It's time to take a break if it is convenient. But before that, General, on transcript page 25 and line 5, you testified that you know after the actual fire, meaning air-strike, members of UNPROFOR came to these positions to see what the effect of the fire were. Could you expand on that? Who did what? Where? Do you have some specific reports of such incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have in mind this last story of mine or something I had said before? I need a time reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said that -- when asked about the report dated 27th of May, you said that you were not sure if the UNPROFOR members was acting as an air controller, but you added that there were incidents that UNPROFOR members came to the sites to confirm the result of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have proof. The bombing began on the 24th of May. It lasted on the 24th, 25th, and 26th of May. My reaction followed the -- the end of that operation. NATO did not interrupt their operation out of mercy for the Serbs but because they could no longer sustain losses. To be specific, my statement that UNPROFOR members attended the scene of combat, following that combat to ascertain effects, and they did so as early as the 24th of May when the bombing began. A few minutes before it all began, I was called by General Rupert Smith for the first and last time. We had never been in contact before. He told me, Unfortunately, General, I cannot change that decision. We will begin striking. It wasn't clear to me at all why he called me and not Karadzic, Mladic, or someone else. I told him, General, you did your part, and let me do mine. A few minutes after the first strikes at Jahorinski Potok, which was a warehouse at Pale, a lieutenant who commanded the warehouse facility called me. He told me that two missiles had hit the target which was the entry to the facility and another building and that eight sheep that were grazing around the facility were killed and that his guard dogs are going crazy because of the blasts. He also told me that he captured eight soldiers of the Russian UNPROFOR contingent and that he tied them to the nearby lightning rods around the warehouse. I went completely mad. I told him, How can you can you tie up living people? And he said, General, no worries. I had report it had to General Rupert Smith first and then I called you. I asked him to release them, but the lieutenant was quite far from me. I reported it to the supreme commander, and Mr. Karadzic started shouting at me to deal with it, especially because the soldiers in question were Russian, and indeed they were released later that afternoon. That is my proof that UNPROFOR could ascertain the effects of their strikes. I did not assert that they guided fire because I didn't see that. I did not have such knowledge. I do know, however, that UNPROFOR through or around or released radio location devices around bridges, such as a small bridge at Bisina. A radio locater is a type of device which guides Tomahawk missiles. They were used on en masse when Serbia was bombed in 1999. I hope this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, General, did you mean to say that those eight Russian UNPROFOR soldiers were there to ascertain the effects of air-strike.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the lieutenant's words, when they arrived, they first wanted to know what happened and what the damage was. They wanted to know whether the missiles had struck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for 20 minutes and resume at 10 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, we have received a translation of the last document, but we haven't had the time to upload it. Could we place it on the ELMO instead and have it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we have English translation which can be confirmed to be the correct one, there's no need to mark it for identification. Could you bring it to Mr. Nicholls so that he can confirm whether it is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 30th of August, 02/2/281.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sure it's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, could we briefly discuss the topic of Sarajevo. Could we have 1D05411 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder the LiveNote for parties are working or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not for me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we can follow in the common monitor, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It is for me now, Your Honours. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mine is also working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mine is not working, but I don't have time to control the transcript anyhow. So 1D05411, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a document pertains to your request to UNPROFOR to establish a joint commission since the Muslims have accused us of having targeted Markale. It says January, but I think it should be February. So the 5th of February. That's the date of the document. In item 1, you see: [In English] "Establish immediately a mixed expert military commission of the representatives of UNPROFOR, the Army of Republika Srpska and the so-called Army of BH, which will at the latest at 0800 hours on the 6th of January," I suppose it's February, "under the protection of UNPROFOR begin to establish the ballistic and every other circumstances ..." [Interpretation] And so on: Item 2: [In English] [As read] "The role of the mixed expert, military commission has to be documented (TV camera, photo shot, sketches, scan, and so on) with all the necessary facts and figures. "The results and the findings of the mixed expert military commission, as soon as it finishes, must be presented to the world public before." [Interpretation] Page 2, please. In item 5: [In English] "If you do not accept our request for establishing the mixed exert military commission, the Army of Republika Srpska will stop every co-operation with UNPROFOR and the humanitarian organisations until the case is objectively and completely explained and the world public informed." [Interpretation] General, is it correct that we did not try to avoid this? Quite the opposite. We demanded an investigation because we were an interested party and we wanted to take part.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it would be better if I told you what took place that afternoon, and I believe through that exercise you may receive some follow-up questions you may have intended to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope I will be accorded a couple of minutes more by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime late in the afternoon on the 5th of February, I was called by the UNPROFOR Chief of Staff for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. -- actually, General Agnes Ramsey [as interpreted]. He told me, General your Serbs created a massacre today at the market-place in Markale. When I asked him what it was about, he said that the Serbs used a mortar shelf 82-millimetre calibre to kill 96 Muslim civilians and wounded 213 civilians. I asked him if he is a professional or a contracted general. He said that he was a professional and that when we met we exchanged CVs and that we rose through the ranks in almost the same way. He was one year older, so to say, in terms of rank as compared to me. I told him that I did not claim the Serbs had not done it, but that I was surprised that in such a small area there were so many people. There is a ballistic law or rule which is that an 82-millimetre mortar shell, as well as a defensive hand grenade, create the same effect upon explosion if the density of people at the impact site is bigger than four persons per square metre, which means they literally have to stand shoulder to shoulder. In such a case, a shell like that kills seven to eight people and wounds 16 to 18 people, whereas any other people that may be there are protected by the bodies of the killed and wounded. He told me something to this effect: You can say or believe what you want, but the Serbs did it. I went back to my argument that I did not claim that the Serbs did not do it, and I offered what we can see in the document. I offered that he, I, and one of the Chiefs of Staff of the so-called Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if possible, not Jovan Divjak because he is a Serb, attend the scene the next morning, since this was in the evening of the 5th of February already. We were to go there together with ballistic experts in order to ascertain objectively who did that. I asked him not to accused the Serbs publicly before that. He asked me, and I don't know whether he was being cynical as it all went through an interpreter, but he was quite insolent when he asked me whether I dared go to Sarajevo. I told him that I would, because it was his duty to protect me. He said it was fine. He also said that I should wait at the forest ranger's house at 8.00 in the morning at Trebevic. They usually waited there for us to take us to any negotiations in Sarajevo itself. I believed it to be an arrangement. However, since I did not trust that general much, I was afraid that he would share that information with his boss, so I drafted the document before us, and I trust what Mr. Karadzic read out. I believe it is accurate. I wrote the document and sent it to the BiH UNPROFOR commander, because both Mladic and Karadzic were in Geneva or London that day at peace talks. I asked General Rose -- or, rather, the UNPROFOR command to provide me with an answer until -- before 6.30 p.m. I did not receive a reply. Somewhere past midnight, at around 2.00 in the morning, General Ramsey called me, and he said, General, there will be no visit of ours. My boss wouldn't have it. I don't know whether he meant Rose or Valgren.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted and then we'll show the next document which speaks about this subsequent phone call of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D5412.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this is your communique following the cancellation of your visit? You say that General Ramsey stated that the Muslim side refused to take part in the formation and work of the joint expert commission. Towards the end, it says the UNPROFOR command refuses that the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR and the Chief of Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Chief of Staff of the VRS attend the scene together in order to establish the facts and consequences of this tragedy. General, did we have the right to participate and be familiar with the results of this investigation, or we were to reject the -- reject any guilt for this act unless we were allowed to take part?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2183, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5414, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again I have only the English version, but I think you can remember that you wrote to General Rose again on the 27th of May, 1994, and you were bitter because -- and you were also concerned because of the increasing -- increasingly frequent violations of the truce by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And here you can see that it says that you were bitter by the extremely false and abject behaviour of the -- it would be better if I read it out in English: [In English] [As read] "I am embittered and extremely -- by extremely false and abject behaviour of the Muslim side in the area of Sarajevo. On one hand they demand Sarajevo to be a safe area, ask protection and special measures, sign the cease-fire; whilst on the other hand they open the fire towards Serb territory, most often uncontrolled and against the urban settlements and civilian population, carry out unprovoked attacks, move their positions by digging roads and trenches, move and regroup their troops and violate the agreed cease-fire on the -- in other ways. I am embittered because such a behaviour causes Serb population suffering and material destroying." [Interpretation] Item 2 says that you were disappointed by UNPROFOR's inability to undertake effective and adequate measures and so on and so forth. General, my question now is whether we ever intended to terrorise the civilians in the Muslim part of Sarajevo. Did we ever do this in any manner, through sniper fire, through use of the artillery? Was this a plan of ours and did we act in accordance with such a plan?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, is it true that in Sarajevo the Muslim artillery often used more projectiles than we did, and many of the projectiles that they fired were, in fact, attributed to our side?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to reports from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command, yes, but as a witness, this is not something I can confirm or deny, because I was not an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this particular case, in the case of Markale, did the Serb side launch an investigation, because initially you did not dismiss the possibility of doing this. So did our army carry out an investigation into whether our side opened fire and, if so, what were the results of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our commission carried out the investigation under the leadership of Colonel Ljuban Kosovac. He was a member of that mixed military group or commission that had been established for the Sarajevo area, and he used his prerogative to enter Sarajevo. There's a detailed report drafted by that group in this book that has been admitted into evidence. This commission was somewhat unsettled by the loss of that mine stabiliser, because it was first recorded as Muslim evidence. It had been dug out from a depth of 25 centimetres in the ground, and later it disappeared. The commission's position in general was that it wasn't a projectile that had come from the Serbian side. And second position was that the explosion hadn't been caused by a shell, a grenade. The position was that the explosion occurred at the level of the ground. And I can't remember the number and date of that report, but it is referred to in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D5171, and I'd ask the Chamber and the OTP for their indulgence and for their understanding in showing these documents I need to show, because General Milovanovic knows much about our war, about our crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a book by General Rasim Delic. Could we now see page -- well, it's the second page in the e-court system. Could we have a look at the right side, page 101. Could we zoom in. General, I'll read this out. It says: The looting on the 24th of October announced that the situation be increasingly complex for the passage of the convoy with arms and equipment for the ABiH through territory under HVO control. Local HVO control against ABiH units were likely to escalate. In addition, given our previous experience of an attempt of raising the blockade showed that the ammunition was being used irrationally. Use of Prazina; for example, in one day fired from Igman about 300, 130-millimetre shells on enemy targets. These features could have been targeted with 82 or 120-millimetre mortars. Similarly, in two or three days' time, from Igman, several thousand 120-millimetre shells were fired from Igman. That's twice as many as could be set aside for other army units, and so on and so forth. So where could these shells from Igman have fallen? And these 130-million howitzer shells, where could they have fallen, General? Only on the Serbian part of Sarajevo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Muslim artillery weren't trained, as was the case for my men, many of those shells could also have fallen on parts of Sarajevo that were under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You know the practice of the Tribunal, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D5414. I think that was the previous one. I apologise. Could we see 1D5415. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document of yours dated the 22nd of July, 1994. You mentioned the area of Sarajevo where Muslim forces have intensified provocative and other action. Then you mentioned these various places. Are these all Serbian places in Sarajevo, General: Grbavica Rajlovac, Vogosca, Nedzarici, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to have to skip many documents that you drafted. Could we see 1D5417, please. And while waiting, General, is it correct that in Sarajevo there were 50- to 70.000 Serbs who lived under Muslim control, and in terms of the way in which they were dressed, in terms of the way that they looked, it was impossible to distinguish them from Muslims? You could not identify them as Serbs in the street.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that there were Serbs in that area, 22 times 11 kilometres, that segment, but I can't say how many. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you, even if we were criminals, would we have terrorised the population -- or, rather, if we had terrorised the population, the civilians, would we have terrorised those thousands of Serbs in Sarajevo, too, and does this make the claim that we did this even more incredible?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere I wrote or somewhere I stated that we couldn't open fire on such parts of town because we didn't know how many Serbs there were in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll up, please. Here you informed the UNPROFOR command on everything, on the violations of the agreement, and here you say in the Sarajevo area the Muslim forces carried out provocative action. They used snipers along all the lines of demarcation, especially from Igman, Stupski, Butmir, Dobrinja, and so forth -- and so on and so forth. Can you tell the Chamber, as briefly as possible, something about the Muslim snipers, and what sort of actions did they undertake in relation to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They -- in that book of mine that you have admitted, I found a piece of information, according to which the Muslims first -- were the first to use snipers in Sarajevo. On the other hand, the Muslims -- or, rather, there was a factory called Zrak that remained under their control, and as early as April, they took about 540 sniper rifles. The factory continued to function during the war. It produced sniper rifles, mostly for the needs of the Muslim army. And while I was saying this, I remembered where I noticed that the Muslims were the first to use snipers. They used snipers when attacking the command of the 2nd Military District. That was on the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. For the sake of the transcript, I'd like to clarify the following: Did you want to say that they started using snipers before the Serbs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started using them when they first took action against the JNA, when they took action against the command of the 2nd military district. So this was some -- well, about a month and a half before the Serbs started using such means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, General, the book wasn't admitted, so there's some important documents of yours that I will have to skip given the time that I still have at my disposal unless I am allocated additional time. Could we see 5159, please. This is your book. 1D5159. That's the first page, the title page of your book. Could we have a look at page 7. I don't know which page it is in the e-court system. It's the introduction. You can see it here. It's the first page in the Serbian version, and it's the first page in the English version too. And here it says that there are 55.000 captives and other Serbs in Sarajevo and other large places of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then 536 Muslim camps for Serbs, and there are 26 such dungeons in Sarajevo. General, did we know that in Sarajevo, apart from the tunnel, the basement, the central prison -- prison in Viktor Bubanj barracks, did we know that there were also private prisons where anyone who wanted to could keep Serbs imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to skip some pages, although it would really be a good thing if the Trial Chamber had the entire book. Can we have page 14 from the book? Yes. It's here. After "Gavrilo Princip," you say: "We were first attacked by mortar fire from the brewery on the 22nd of April, 1992." And then a bit further down you say, as you said, on the 2nd of May there was an attack using all kinds of weapons, and so on and so forth. Then also tear-gas was used, power was cut, water, telephone lines, a truck full of explosives. General, actually, all of this, was this not repetition of all those things that had been done against JNA barracks in Slovenia and particularly Croatia? Were lives of people truly threatened? And you say further down that you could have lost your life three times on that day yourself. In English it's page 3, actually.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is testimony of a lieutenant-colonel because I didn't take part in this. The name rings a bell. If the Trial Chamber wishes for me to do so, I can refer to the man's name and surname, but we have to do this in private session, because when I was writing the book the man asked me not to disclose his name because part of his family still lives in the Muslim area -- or, rather, in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Until the Trial Chamber decides whether we are going to move into private session, I am going to say in support of this that this is an absolute copy of the tactics that were applied by Croatia -- or, rather, in Croatia against members of the JNA, and I know with full certainty that the Patriotic League sent their own chosen men, special forces, for training in Croatia in 1991; so a year before the conflict broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They completed their special forces training and they returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Sarajevo, for this kind of activity, blockades, power cuts, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Trial Chamber is interested in the name of this officer, we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's for you, Mr. Karadzic, to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, please, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: By the way, where do we find that passage in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3. That's what it was supposed to be. Page 3, where there's a reference to Gavrilo Princip. It's somewhere around the beginning of the second paragraph: [In English] "... should be examined in brief." [Interpretation] It's around the 12th or 15th line from the top: [In English] "The first we were attacked on mortar fire from the brewery, 22nd of April, 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. In the middle of the last paragraph, yes, if it is correct. Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now ask for page 26 from this book, and the chapter it pertains to is the war objectives of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually -- actually, before the war objectives of the warring parties, do we agree that this is what it says here: On the 2nd of May, all the things that were attacked. Although disagreement had been reached on the 12th of May, the Assembly made a decision to establish the army. On the 26th -- or, rather, I think on the 27th of May -- it's actually the next page. Twenty-seven. In English it's page 5. You are saying that that round of talks failed because of Vasa Miskin in Crni -- or, rather, the shell that allegedly fell there, and then on the 4th of August war was declared on the Serbs. Do you agree that the first declaration of war against the Serbs was on the 20th of June, 1992. Effective as of the 22nd of June, whereas this is probably ...

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, a state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared on the 4th of August, 1992. Mobilisation was carried out on the 4th of April, 1992, two days before the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And on the 20th of June, Alija Izetbegovic declared war on the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. When war was declared on the Serbs -- or, rather, on Serbia and Montenegro and the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the SAOs, as he said, is Bosnia thereby transformed into a theatre of war? And is the responsibility for that to be borne by the side that declared war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A crime against peace was committed, according to the Charter from 1945, the UN Charter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have page 32 in Serbian now, where you speak about the war objectives of the warring parties. So it's the Serb objectives and the beginning of the Muslim objectives. In English it's page 6. You said here for the Serbs: "The objectives were to remain part of Yugoslavia so that both the Serbs in BH and equally those in Croatia would not become national minorities ... so that all Serbs would live in one state in the Balkans as a constituent people." And you say: "As by different tricks, roses [as interpreted] and deceit, the Muslim-Croat coalition (and that is the only thing in which they act in unison) and with the blessing of the international community did not allow them to do that. The Serbs resorted to the only option available, namely to defend themselves in territories where they constituted a majority." Do you remember, General, in your interview to the OTP on the 27th of March -- actually, 2001. You said in response to the question that had been put to you, What were the tasks put before the military by the political leadership, you referred to two tasks, to save people from genocide and to keep the territory until a political solution is found. Is that in accordance with what is written here, and do you confirm this today as well?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Towards the bottom, it says for the Muslims.
