First they agreed to remain in Yugoslavia, and then -- and then "they changed their mines," under quotation marks, and their objective was to create an Islamic state in the territory of Europe, and do we agree that that conclusion is indubitably drawn from Mr. Izetbegovic's Islamic Declaration?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have page 35. Seven in English. You say that the main cause of the war conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina lies in the attempt of the Muslim-Croat coalition to forcibly lead the Serbian people out of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the Serbian people from Bosnia-Herzegovina out of Yugoslavia and to establish state domination over it, and you speak about the number of persons that were killed by the Ustasha in the Second World War. General, do you agree - and that is what Lord Owen wrote in his book -- book as well, that as soon as World War II insignia appeared in Croatia as manifested by the HDZ and also rhetoric from the Second World War, the Serbs were already in fear, and the place where you were born is on the Croatian border?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to raise a crucial question here. All the representatives of the UN in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this is a question I have for them: Why did they not behave that way when they were there? And then in their memoirs they write the truth? General Rose in his memoirs -- I mean, General Rose did not act the way he wrote his memoirs, and when he testified here he testified again along the lines of what he did while he was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am calling upon them to exhibit their Honour as military men, officers, and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You speak of national armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can we have page 40 now, towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, did you find the passage on page 7 of the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Third paragraph. [In English] "The basic cause ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. Towards the bottom you say this led to the following: The Rump Presidency of the FRY, Slovenia and Croatia had already left, reached agreement with the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina that parts of the JNA remain here for the following five years, that is say until 1997, as a factor of peace among the three peoples. However, the agreement was first violated by the Muslim-Croatian coalition by use of arms against the JNA and declaring -- and declaring mobilisation of their constituent peoples. Can we have the next page in Serbian. In English the page is fine. And then the FRY, the decision of the withdrawal of Montenegrins, and Serbs from JNA unit with the dead-line for compliance being the 19th of May, 1992, so Serbs in BH, both as civilians and as soldiers, were betrayed by both sides. The Muslim-Croat alliance committed that betrayal by declaring war on the Serbs, and the FRY left us without protection. General, it is correct that the Serb side said that they had the right to remain in the federal state -- or, rather, that they had the right for the federal state to defend them, protect them? The Muslim leadership, already on the 23rd of December, 1991, do you remember that? They asked the JNA -- at this meeting with the JNA, they asked for the JNA to remain as a factor of peace in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is the reason why the Serb side was the last one to establish its own army as the 7th armed force in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Another thing, the armed forces of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in addition to the Macedonian army, are the only armed force that did not take political power; rather, they committed themselves to defending it. All other armed forces created in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that is to say Slovenia, Croatia, and the Muslim-Croat coalition, brought their own political leaderships to power. That is to say the Serb armed forces -- or, rather, the Army of Republika Srpska was a defensive army with a defensive strategy, from a strategic point of view. And, of course, active combat activities, minor ones, were only engaged in with a view to improving one's own positions. I have to say one more thing. Not a single activity of the Army of Republika Srpska, starting with platoons all the way up to the level of brigades and corps, up to the army as a whole, was not carried out without having been provoked beforehand. That is explained in this book starting with Operation Corridor in 1992 and finally the counter-attack in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These were counter-offensives; right? If you agree, General. Our actions were always responses to threats.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terms, that is termed responses to challenges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at page 43 now. While we're waiting, General, perhaps I asked you this already: Can we agree that all seven armies were borne out of the JNA, the officers, the reservists? Is it true that the JNA is the mother and mainstream of all of those seven armies?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 9 in English, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA and the TO of the SFRY were the backbone used to create all the armed forces in the territory of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The fact that the Muslims and Croats saw many people join their armies, thus creating a false impression that the JNA became an armed force of the VRS only because it took place at once and not gradually as was the case with the other armed forces. In other words, whatever was left is what we kept as ours.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It can be demonstrated by looking at the creation of the 1st Corps of the Army of BiH in Sarajevo and our Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The military equipment and weapons were practically divided in two, but the Muslims had taken their weapons by force from the JNA, whereas the VRS simply kept certain assets without any use of violence as the JNA was withdrawing. Not a single JNA member was killed in order to keep a howitzer or a gun behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under (a) on this page you say that the Muslim army was being formed and people were leaving the JNA to join it as early as 1991 and 1992. On the next page you discuss criminals and gangs which established the Patriotic League. Can we go to the next page in Serbian. They also created the Green Berets and also several smaller militant, paramilitary groups such as Jamiski Golubovi [phoen], Laste, Seve, the jihad warriors, et cetera, and all those groups united again the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you can see that in his book, too. Rasim Delic addresses the criminal groups of Juka Prazina and others in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Rasim Delic also informed us that the criminal in question, Juka Prazina, had 3.000 shells at his disposal which he fired in only two days? So the criminal was part and parcel of the Muslim army. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that as well, that upon formation the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina kept the military groups -- the paramilitary groups which reported to -- directly to the staff and the Supreme Command of the Muslim army rather than the corps. In other words, the supreme corps command was aware of their existence and supplied ammunition and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that the Croats and Muslims joined together against the Serbs, thus forming the well-known Serb-Croat Muslim coalition, but the very next year Serbs had to pull many of them out by their roots and vehicles from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember that we were trying to save Croats from the Lasva valley and there were tens of thousands of them? We fed the Croats in Vares and transported them to Kiseljak. We took Croats from Konjic as well; in other words, we often played UNPROFOR in this conflict between Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you, too, should recollect that we all had, too -- had arguments about that, you and I. We were feeding and helping them at the same time when they were attacking us in such areas where they were not under Muslim attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 45 in the Serbian, which is the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is one paragraph which is particularly interesting to me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic provide an exact reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this: Do you agree that the following model existed: First, Serbs were terrorised for almost a year. Monuments to writers were destroyed such as to Copic and Andric? Then, at the very beginning of the war, Serbs were attacked and our civilians and men for -- fit for military service fled. What followed was the return of the men fit for military service and combat. Such was the case with Zvornik where the Serbs had initially fled as well as from Bratunac, Visegrad, Foca, and there was similar scenarios and other places. After a year-long campaign of terror, it seemed that they won the first round after which the Serbs returned and there was combat. Does this reflect what you know about the period, and was this model followed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have such knowledge, but I'm not certain about the model itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here you write about the 1st Corps, which used Serbs in Sarajevo en masse as a human shield, and that some 10.000 Sarajevo Serbs went missing or were killed. And if we go by first and last names, some 8.000 people have been identified so far as Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote this in 2005 when we still didn't know the exact number of missing Serbs in Sarajevo. In the meantime, the fate of many was discovered. I even mentioned somewhere that an additional 5- to 8.000 Serbs were still missing, whereas the figure now stands at only some 200. So, for the most part, my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, can you tell me how much time I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much do you need to conclude, Mr. Karadzic? It's about time for you to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's why I'm asking. If I could have at least half an hour, but I could use an hour as this is an invaluable witness. I would need a lot of time to go through his documents alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the circumstances regarding the courtroom today, in particular that another trial that involves Judge Lattanzi starts only 3.00, the Chamber has decided, upon the agreement of staff, that we will go till 2.30 or 2.40 today, and we'll extend this session to 20 past 12.00. So, Mr. Karadzic, please conclude your cross-examination by that time. You have 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. You're full of understanding in the case of this witness. Thank you. Can we go to page 48 of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I lost track of following the passage in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stevanovic will assist us all. The page we have had before was good, and I believe we'll be able to find the right now one as well. We're looking for item (c) in the Serbian, the Army of Republika Srpska. Yes. Here we have paragraph (c).

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There you write, General, that the last seven in a row, national armed force to be formed was the VRS. And you wonder why it had not been done before, and you find only one reason, which is the attempts of the political leadership and the Serbian people as a whole to work out the situation so as to avoid an armed conflict between the three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you agree that we all hoped we could get away without a war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 59 in the Serbian, please, and we'll locate the right page in English. Towards the bottom you discuss the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic wait for the interpreters until we find the right piece of text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] Here we have the examples --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 12 in the English. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the middle, we see Corridor 92. Here, you summarise the motive and our responses. The Corridor 92 operation was provoked by an operation against Banja Luka. Then under 2, Operation Podrinje 93 was a response to the massacres of Serbs in Kamenica, Cerska, Kravica, Bratunac, Skelani, and different villages at mount Sjiemic [phoen]. Under 3, Operation Lukavac 93 was a response to the occupation of Trnovo Rogoj, et cetera, and the massacres of Serbs in the villages around Foca and Trnovo. 4, the VRS counter-attack towards Bihac in November 1994 was an answer to the counter-strike of the Muslims from that area. General, we had only four large operations, and all were a matter of life and death for us, for without them we would not have survived. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were the four offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in Sarajevo the front lines remained more or less in the same positions as they had been established by the Serb TO forces when engaging the paramilitary groups there? The only changes that took place were minor and were to the benefit of the Muslims and say -- and we didn't take many parts of Sarajevo, although we could have.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 62, please. The chapter about the plight of civilians as a general category, not only Serb civilians. Page 13 in the English. This is the right chapter. There you discuss the accusations against us, such as the shelling of Sarajevo, et cetera. Civilians, especially Serbs in Sarajevo, suffered, although when referred to victims in general, only Muslims are referred to by their international patrons. 150.000 Serbs fled from Sarajevo and over 2.000 of them went missing. Do you agree, General, that throughout the war the figure of between 300.000 and 350.000 killed Muslims was something that was frequently heard? And about 80.000 or 60.000 raped Muslim women. It was all in the function of waging war. As it turns out, there were only 17 or 18 Muslim women who had been raped, whereas there were more Serb women who had been raped, and the overall losses amounted to about 100.000.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember Haris Silajdzic's statement in Vienna. I don't know the date. He said that the VRS raped 150.000 Muslim women. That evening, my courier asked me who raped his Muslim woman, because he had not raped any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you're trying to say if we go by the figures, he would have raped one; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can find an official report issued by the Muslim Supreme Command dated the 31st of August, 1994, which reads the Muslim army in the past 29 months of war lost 235.627 fighters. If anyone were to analyse this rationally, what were their total figures of fighters when international standards say that any military formation which lost over 40 per cent of personnel is considered neutralised, incapable of fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just wonder if we're going to get any basis for the conclusion put out that there were only 17 or 18 Muslim women who had been raped during the course the entire war?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will show that today. We don't have time now, but we will show that international commissions were able to register only as few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That all boils down to the efficiency of your cross-examination. It's all worthless statements coming from you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll restrain myself. Can we see the next page here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You speak about murders and setting up your own population to die --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just refrain, but when you referred to the previous passage, did you say 2.000 of them went missing out of 150.000 fled?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to the Serbs, 150.000 fled and 10.000 went missing or were killed. And that's what it says here on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you said 2.000 missing. That's -- in the -- in this page, General, you said 10.000 of those who fled Sarajevo proven to have been killed and those 5- to 7.000 nothing is known of. So when you say 10.000 of those proven, what did you mean by "proven"? What proof do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I don't understand your question, but this is what I said: About 150.000 Serbs were driven out of Sarajevo, and more than 10.000 have been provable to have been killed, and about 5- to 7.000, well, nothing is known about them. I apologise for mentioning the figure of 2.000, but I said that out of that figure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. General Milovanovic, it was not you that mentioned 2.000, but my question is: What did you mean by "being proven" that 10.000 people have been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two commissions working on this evidence in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Their figures are not totally identical. I don't know within which context I mentioned the figure of 2.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it at that. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can be of assistance, General. You said you wrote the book in 2005, and at the time there were 5- to 7 .000 missing, and you said that out of those 5- to 7.000, now, one doesn't know anything about the fate of 2.000 of them. You rely on the information of the commissions with regard to the figures on those who were killed. Is it true that in Sarajevo there is an association of Serbs that is involved in carrying out such investigations and it is from this association that these figures were obtained?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm claiming, yet again, that I said that searches are still being conducted for 1.200-odd individuals. Two thousand, I don't know where I got that figure from, but this figure is one that I got from the association of families for those who went missing in Republika Srpska. I think Mitrovic was at the head of that commission, and that was information from him. Searches were still being conducted in order to locate about 1.200 Serbs whose fate remains unknown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. So I would like you to spend the remaining time efficiently on relevant issues. You have five minutes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can't deal with the whole book, but in general terms, General, is it correct that for the purpose of various conferences or for other needs the Muslim side sacrificed its own people in order to tarnish our image and to gain the international community's sympathy?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by everything that I stated in this book that concerns the Vaske Miskin Street and Markale I, as well. I'm not sure about Markale II. Furthermore, wherever I stated that the Muslims wanted to interrupt the conference if the Serbs seemed to be in a better position, or if they rejected what the Serbs were saying, well, gentlemen, somewhere I said -- I wrote that the Muslims accepted the Dayton agreement because they were counting on the Serbs not respecting it. That's what Rasim Delic said in Tehran in the period from the time the Dayton agreement was reached up until the time that it was signed in Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I have another three minutes, so if you agree with my questions, please answer by just saying yes or no. In the case of Markale II, are you not certain about that case because you weren't there, but you were in the western part of Republika Srpska at the time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Markale II provoked that 17-day period of NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you ever hear about or even participate or support, but did you ever hear about us having a project according to which we should expel the Muslims or Croats in the territory in which we were in the majority? So did you ever hear about such a project, not to say participate in such a project or support it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard about such a project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that their entire villages and hamlets with Muslim inhabitants and in Serbian towns there were always Muslims right up until the end of the war, especially Muslims who didn't have family members in the ABiH? They remained there and lived with us until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, the Satorovici village near Rogatica could be an example; another example would be Janja in Bijeljina; another example would be Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in Gradiska, Srbac, Derventa, Kobas, Dubocac, and so on and so forth; isn't that right? Kobas, Dubocac, and in Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the inhabited places I am sure of. These are places that I visited in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You mentioned the attack of a village -- on a village. Did the VRS or did some unit act according to an order or with the knowledge of a command to commit a crime? Did any such unit act in order to conceal the perpetrators of a crime? Are you aware of the fact that some unit from the VRS -- I'm not talking about individuals or personal vendettas. Are you aware of any units acting in a criminal manner and attempting to conceal the crimes perpetrated? Are you familiar with any such cases?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, were our military courts fully operational during that period of time and was everything documented so that proceedings are now instituted on the basis of the documents that relate to crimes committed by individuals in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that these things were documented, but I'm not really familiar with the operations of the military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But during the war, the military courts functioned all the time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you can answer the question. I'll hear from you afterwards. Yes, please answer the question, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have answered the question. Everything was documented, but I'm not sure that the courts functioned continually because I didn't monitor the situation throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had no objection. It's just in the question at line 61 [sic]. From what I heard in my headphones, I think something got missed in the transcript, if I'm correct, which is that Mr. Karadzic said to the effect of courts were fully operational during that period of time and everything was documented so that proceedings are now being instituted. In other words, are happening now. That's missing from the question, unless I misheard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we haven't yet spoken about the Sanski Assembly. You weren't there. I don't think you were there. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were. General, do we agree that the words spoken in the heat of that political combat shouldn't be taken literally? Such words should be taken cum grano salis, given that it's all a matter of political speeches and exaggerations. Such words should be taken with a grain of salt.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there was more political exaggeration than military exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I hope we won't have to call you for the Defence case, and I apologise for being somewhat confused on occasion because of my desire to obtain as much information from you as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, we'll have a break for 40 minutes. So we'll resume at five past 1.00 and then we'll have about 90 minutes session. You'll have more than 30 minutes, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because of the schedule that Mr. Tieger spoke about, I'll be as -- as brief as possible, because we are under some constraints for the next couple days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hmm, yes. Very well, 40 minutes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have limited time, so please try to answer briefly, if you can. The first thing I want to ask you about is something you said about Sarajevo. This is at T-25690, and it refers to the conversation you had with General van Baal about sniping when you said words to the effect of I can't prevent some idiot from shooting. Now, in the transcript, at line 19 of that page, you say: "The soldier who was closest to Marin Dvor was 5.5 kilometres away, which -- what kind of sniper can fire on targets 5.5 kilometres away?" Do you remember that, talking about that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 12446, please. While that's coming up, this is a document from the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade command dated 3 September 1992, and it's signed -- we don't need to go to the last page now, but it's signed by Dragomir Milosevic. Could I go to page 4 of the English. And it should be page 2 of the Serbian language, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now what I'm asking about, General, is the line and where some of the VRS forces are deployed according to this document: "The 1st pb is defending the following front line: Metalka, left bang of the Miljacka River up to Strorjorad the right side of Duraskovica street ..." Do you see that in your version? I think it's under point 2, 2.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it the second paragraph where it says the 2nd Infantry Battalion or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Metalka, left bank of the Miljacka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Exactly. Now I'd like to show you 23643, please. That's a photograph, General. And while it's coming up, I will tell you that this is a photo taken from the Metalka building. And do you recognise the building we see through the window with some yellow facade on it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be told what the scale is, how much this has been enlarged? It's not the normal scale, this photograph taken from Metalka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a normal photograph taken from Metalka so the scale is whatever a camera captured when it's just taking a normal photo. And I will show another picture in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can see the frame of the building. Do you recognise the building with the yellow facade, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with Sarajevo. I don't know Sarajevo, but I think this is the Holiday Inn Hotel, which I saw after the war. So on the basis of the front of the building, I assume that it is the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Now could I show 23641, please. Maybe this photo will help Mr. Karadzic. This is a photograph taken from the tram tracks we saw in the previous photo toward the Metalka building in the back. My question, General, is you said 5.5 kilometres were the closest snipers. How far away does that building look from the area we just saw by the Holiday Inn? Estimate.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not say the sniper who was furthest away. I said the soldier who was closest to that location was 5.5 kilometres away. Since that is the centre, well, I don't know this building, and judging by the photograph, the distance, as far as I can see, is about a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, General, but I just wonder if your opinion changed at all. If you accept my representation that that's the Metalka building, did not the document we just look at from 3 September signed by Dragomir Milosevic say that that is where the line was being defended?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just ask something? This is the Prosecution's witness. I don't mean to assist, but the gentleman spoke about Marin Dvor, not the Holiday Inn, and in Marin Dvor area, the lines are located on Zlastiste on Trebevic. Not everything should be situated in the Holiday Inn area. The Holiday Inn area and Marin Dvor are not the same areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, we can argue about that later, but the Marin Dvor area is in the vicinity of the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General, can you answer my question, which, before I was interrupted, was that if this is the Metalka building, didn't we see that this is an area that was defended by VRS troops?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question, because van Baal said to me that the tram was at Marin Dvor. Marin Dvor was designated by UNPROFOR as the centre of Sarajevo, the centre of the ellipsis, and my logic was that it was 11 kilometres wide, so the closest soldier of the Army of Republika Srpska could have been only 5.5 kilometres away from that tram that had been hit. So this is a different situation that I was unaware of, and I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would move to admit these three documents, although the witness did dispute the -- whether he was able to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure we need to admit it, but do you have any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I don't think they've met the qualifications for admission, but if you think it would assist you to understand his answers, we don't really have a problem for context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have not already a sufficient number of photos regarding these incidents, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you brought me to my next question, General, which is about the ellipsis --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I'm so sorry. If the Prosecution does not wish to tender that report, the Defence would like to tender General Milosevic's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering that report, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 12446. Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You referred to the ellipsis just now --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a second. As Exhibit P4498, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As well at page 41 today, and I just wanted to ask you a question about that, those dimensions. Could I have D718, please. Excuse me. It's D718. That's it. Thank you. And if we can blow-up in the centre a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, looking at this centre where we have 1K for the 1st Corps and the lines drawn there around Sarajevo, is this shape we see in the centre marked 1K encircled in the blue and red, is that the ellipsis you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The blue does not resemble an ellipsis. However, the yellow, I don't know why it's yellow. That is what -- is more reminiscent of an ellipsis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So my question is the 11 by 22 ellipse that you've referred to on a few occasions is greater than what we see in this 1K -- this area marked 1K. Is that -- do I understand you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that, which is already an exhibit. I'd like to bring up P02955. Now, in your cross-examination at 25560 to 25562, there was a discussion about the sort of great humanitarian of the Drina Corps, Miladen Prstojevic. I just wanted to show you this document dated 17 December 1992. 02955 should be available. Yes. Could we just go to the last page to begin with so that General Milovanovic can see who signed it. All right. We can go back to the first page now. In both languages. And scroll down. The third paragraph there, can you read that to yourself and I'll read out the English. I'm only interested in the first part: "With the arrival of paramilitary organisations to the Zvornik municipality, particularly the arrival of Arkan and his people, the territory was liberated from the Turks. Turks made up 60 per cent of the municipality's population and it has now been cleansed and replaced with an ethnically pure Serb population." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we kindly ask Mr. Nicholls to ask the witness to go on reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I know what Mr. Karadzic is getting at, I think. The continuation of the paragraph shows: Problems caused by the paramilitaries which are now taking place in this ethnically pure Serb municipality, thievery, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, my question is: You spoke a lot about this man Miladen Prstojevic and his humanitarian bent. Do you see anything where he speaks negatively about the fact there that the municipality is now a hundred per cent Serb? Is that the way you view it? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that Colonel Prstojevic was a big-time humanitarian as you've been claiming, but I said that he was one of the more literate officers that I sent to the Drina Corps to conceptualise the work of the corps at the time. When Prstojevic wrote this, if I'm not mistaken, this is the 17th of December, 1992, Colonel Prstojevic was commander of the outer ring for the protection of the Main Staff. At that time, from the 11th to the 16th of December, the Main Staff was attacked by a sabotage terrorist group that had infiltrated the area, and no one took responsibility for their deeds and misdeeds; the Muslims or the HVO, no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you an sec, and go to the back page so you can see what the stamp says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can zoom in on it, can we?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Does that help you with his position at the time he wrote this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I've said that he's an operations officer in the Drina Corps, the head of the organ for operations and training --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to get that this was the Drina Corps, not Main Staff. I don't want to cut you off. Did you have something else you needed to finish? I just wanted to show you that stamp first.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at T-25572, Mr. Karadzic said: "It is my intention to show you documents and to show you that directive 4, whatever its contents, had no negative consequences for the civilians on the ground." So I want to look at some documents from the Drina Corps after directive 4 was issued and after Zivanovic's order implementing directive 4 was issued that we looked at. The first one is 65 ter 30868. This is an intercept from 8 February 1993. The speakers are Zivanovic and Gaborovic. It's the one that begins at 10.45. Okay. Read it to yourself, please, General, and then I'll ask you to read out loud the last three lines spoken by Zivanovic, who we say is Milenko Zivanovic, and Gaborovic. And the parts I'm talking about where Zivanovic starts saying "Hold tight the positions," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, but it would be a good thing if you could zoom in a bit. It's very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. What it says in my translation is: "Hold tightly the positions. Are the Turks' houses burning?" And Gaborovic then says: "They are burning. They are burning." And the commander of the Drina Corps says: "Way to go. As many as possible." Is that what it says in your language in the original Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just very simply, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I don't know who this Gaborovic is. According to what Zivanovic is saying to him, I assume that he's an engineering man, because he is asking him to have some obstacles placed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we ask Mr. Nicholls what this has to do with directive 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Directive 4 is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, and I -- there have been quite a few interruptions so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, General, just very quickly, in your view as an officer, a life-long military man and an officer on the Main Staff, does this statement and what we see here from the Drina Corps commander imply negative consequences for civilians?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the date of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's the 8th of February, 1993, Your Honours, and you can't see that on that page, but if we go back in the transcript, and I'm not sure if all the pages in the transcript are in e-court, but I have a hard copy. We can see that it's the 8th of February, 1993. Do we have a previous page in e-court in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We have only one page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can put the previous page on the ELMO, if Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It won't be necessary. We take your word. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We object to the admission or the marking for identification of this intercept. The witness hasn't confirmed anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the witness knows who commander -- Drina Corps commander Zivanovic is and knows that this is a date shortly after directive 4 was issued during the period of Proboj. I think it can at least be marked for identification. I wasn't going to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused, Mr. Nicholls. If you're not going to tender it, what's the point of marking it for identification at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender it, Your Honour, but we don't have either interlocutor here at the moment. I would tender it, but perhaps with a different witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, why don't you tender it when you use it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd now like to show you, General, 21259. This is a short time later, ten days later, 18th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we go to the second page, perhaps, of the Serbian or the bottom so that the General can see who signed it or whose name it is under. Could we scroll down to the bottom. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while we're here, maybe you could read just to yourself paragraph 5, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read this, but I don't understand what the significance of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go to the first page. First of all, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my document judging by the number 02, and also the signature. However, it was sent by teleprinter, hence there is no handwritten signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the relevance I'm getting to now is this is based on directive 4, the amendment to directive 4 from 7 December and the explicit request by the supreme commander. And what we saw in paragraph 5 was that in the supreme commander's opinion, further combat activities and future appearance of RS territory depends on the execution of this task. And then we can see what the tasks are, liberation of Orasje. So my question is looking at this, you talked about how the people in directive 4 meant that once the people moved out, that was your view, then the army should be moved out. What does this document tell us about the supreme commander's view that directive 4 was necessary and crucial -- was necessary to the future appearance of RS territory?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Incomplete. It also says for continuation of struggle, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you are trying to feed the witness. I think General is capable of answering questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no objections as far as the General is concerned. It's Mr. Nicholls who is changing this. He is leaving out parts that are important. In my view, that is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the leading part. Why don't you continue, Mr. Nicholls. What was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General, the question I asked you was: What does this document tell us about the supreme commander's view of the combat operations related to directive 4 regarding, as it says, the future appearance of RS territory?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you will have to allow me to read the document, because this is just an excerpt, paragraph 5, that you asked me about. On the basis of that only, I cannot conclude what the commander had in mind. There's a reference to Orasje and Gradacac here and I do not recall them being mentioned in directive 4. Directive 4 introduced the Drina Corps into the system, the war system of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why don't you read the whole document. You can go to page 1, and when you're done we can go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often you keep changing the page, going up and down, and now it's the last page. Please put the first page first and then I can read it. Yes. This should be right. You can change the page now. I can start answering now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'll ask the question again and try to make it a little clearer. The first paragraph of this document says, and it's to the 1 kk and East Bosnia Corps: Based on directive operative number 4 the amendments to directive 4 and the explicit requests by the supreme commander to carry out the tasks here. And the last paragraph says: In the supreme commander's opinion, future combat activity and future appearance of RS territory depends largely on the execution of this task. So the question is very simply again: What does this tell us about the supreme commander's view that directive 4 related to, put it that way, the future appearance of the RS territory?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directive 4 does not pertain to the future Republika Srpska. However, this document extends -- or, rather, by way of this document, the commander is extending - how should I put this? - the authority of directive number 4. He is of the intent that the territory of Republika Srpska should extend to Orasje and the Sava River valley, whereas in the other parts of the front, Doboj, and whatever else he mentioned, Gradacac and whatever, he asked for enemy forces to be kept there. He is not asking for the taking of new territory. He is asking that the enemy forces be engaged so as not to be able to help them in Orasje and in the Sava River valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You just said directive 4 does not pertain to the future Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have P02085.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I wasn't going to use this, General, but let's look at it again. This is the 24 November 1992 document pursuant to directive 4, signed by General Zivanovic, that we looked at before. And if I go to page 2 of the English and page 3 of the Serbian. Page 2 of the English, please. All right. I'm focusing on the bottom (c), section (c): "Morale and psychological preparations: Before initiating any kind of operation," again, this is pursuant to directive 4, "inform the unit members about the important aim of that operation and underline that the outcome of minor actions and of the whole operation is of crucial importance for the realisation of the aim of the Serbian people, namely the creation and establishment of a Serbian state in these areas." So now I'll just ask you if that -- if you can add to your answer having seen the way the Drina Corps commander viewed directive 4. Does it pertain to the future Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I need to intervene. Have I been accused of establishing Republika Srpska? What sense is there in putting to the witness legitimate orders and present them as a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. Your objection is overruled. Can you answer the question, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was a standard item in all psychological and morale preparations of the army in the execution of a task. The goal is to have each and every soldier be clear about the task. I don't know what the order pertains to directly, but the corps commander is asking his superiors -- his subordinates to acquaint all members of the unit with the importance of the activity and to point out that the entire operation depends on the implementation of even smaller operations which ultimately should lead to the realisation of the aim of the Serbian people which is the creation and establishment of a Serbian state. During my testimony, I said that the political goal of this RS leadership was that if we were unable to remain within Yugoslavia, we could at least be in a position to establish our own ethnic community. I see nothing wrong with the corps commander ordering his subordinate commanders to inform the last soldier in the field with the purpose of this operation so that he should know what it is that he's fighting for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You said you didn't know what this order pertained to directly, this order that President Karadzic just said was legitimate. Let's look at page 1 again, please, the first paragraph. I won't read it out loud again. The first sentence by the number 1 in paragraph 1, do you remember this order now, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on Thursday -- well, during my testimony, in any case, we have already discussed this document, and I believe I found it to be incorrect in terms of directive number 4, because this is the date of directive number 4. Following this document, we looked at a document by Colonel Prstojevic, where he amended this item of the order where it says that the Muslim local population should be forced to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. He invoked international humanitarian law and disseminated it to the soldiers. Colonel Prstojevic took upon himself not to implement the corps commander's order when it came to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me move on to another document, General, P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, are you tendering 65 ter 21259, General Milovanovic's order to SRK and IBK?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted as Exhibit P -- what's the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P4499, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not my order to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and East Bosnia Corps but to the 1st Corps and the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct. My mistake. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Milovanovic. Could I have P03162, please. This is the 2nd of March order by somebody you know, Commander Svetozar Andric. I shouldn't say order, my error. Regular combat report. Just take a look at this, General. The part I'm going to ask you about is this: "Our forces which are moving in the wider area of Kamenica, Gajici, and Grobici worked according to plan without major problems. The village of Gobelji has been burnt and tomorrow the plan is to do Paljevine." And the question I have is the same one I asked you earlier. In your view, does this imply negative consequences for civilians on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Does burning down villages imply negative consequences for civilians on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object to that question as being argumentative. It's practically a rhetorical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you reformulate the question, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General, Mr. Karadzic said to you that he was going to show that directive 4 had no negative consequences for the civilians on the ground. This is from the 2nd of March, 1993. It's in the area spelled out in directive 4. It's after Proboj has begun. Could you give me your comment on the last sentence of paragraph 2: Our forces are moving in the wider area of Kamenica, et cetera. It talked about the burning of the village of Gobelji and that the plan is to do Paljevine the next day.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence is not in the spirit of directive number 4, but is in the spirit of Zivanovic's order which stems from directive 4 that Colonel Prstojevic tried to alleviate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 21929, please. Sorry, 21955.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a special operative report, Drina Corps command, also from 2nd of March, 1993. I'm going to ask you the same question as before about Mr. Karadzic's assertion of directive 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we can scroll down in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We see another reference to the village of Gobelji being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You may have to scroll down for the General, please. Or go to the next page, actually.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part of the text were you interested?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "In the course of the day, special units of the 1st Birac Light Infantry Brigade took and destroyed the village of Gobelji, thus fleeing up the left flank of the main forces in the attack on Cerska." The next page in the Serbian, I think. Should be under the number -- should be the top of page 2 in the Serbian, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Birac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you find the section, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and it reads: "During the day, special units of the 1st Birac Light Infantry Brigade took and destroyed the village of," I can't read the name, "thus freeing up the left flank of our forces -- the left flank of our forces in their attack on Cerska. Upon entering the village, our soldiers came across weapons and other military equipment as well as food and cattle that was left behind by the enemy when fleeing from our troops. Unless the Zvornik Brigade continued their -- continues their attack on the aforementioned facilities or elevations, Udrc will no longer present any danger to any unit." What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. The question is in the document we saw earlier, we saw that Colonel Andric reported that Gobelji has been burnt. In this document we're looking at now, it says this village of Gobelji has been destroyed. Can you comment on the destruction of this village, the burning of this village when the document we see here now says that when the VRS entered the village there was nobody left there, everybody had already left?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any residents mentioned, but I did see in the document that the army had left leaving behind the weapons, ammunition, food, and cattle left behind by the enemy when fleeing. I can only presume that it was a fortified village which became a military facility; much the same way I mentioned the villages of Amcici [phoen] and Delijas, which had been turned into military facilities. Now, whether the Muslims had previously evacuated the civilians or whether the civilians fled together with the army, that's another matter. I suppose that the village was fortified and thus a military target. It was an enemy's resistance point, as we call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But what would be the military justification, if you can explain to us, help us, to burning the village or destroying it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The justification is this: If it is a fortified village, first of all, it became a military target. The houses were turned into bunkers and fortified firing positions. One cannot eliminate a fire position other than destroying it and bringing down its walls. It doesn't say here that they torched it but that they destroyed it. Sir, if we go by the text, we cannot see whether the village had been fortified. If we look at the second part of the sentence that -- that weapons, ammunition, food, and cattle were found, I conclude that it was a military target. It is another matter whether there were civilians there. Why did then the enemy commander allow that civilians mix with the soldiers in a military target?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This was already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. I didn't realise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 21955 has been already assigned Exhibit P3161. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me go to 65 ter 21928, please. 65 ter 21928.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from the 4th of March, 1993, so it's still in the same period. It's a regular combat report from Vinko Pandurevic, who was described by you as a -- I think as a rising star, something like that, in the Drina Corps a couple days ago. And the part I'm interested in is this: "Activity in the direction of Konjevic Polje - Duge Njive - Rasevo. Duge Njive and Glodi have been taken and facilities in Glodi burnt." Tell me when you've had a chance to read the document.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read this. It is too blurry. I can only make out single words. It is unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's try blowing up the section just above number 3. "Activity in the direction of Konjevic Polje," that's the part I'm asking about.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read the part just above number 3 with the white circle. It was probably a hole in the paper so that it could be included in a binder. It says: "Along the axis Konjevic Polje-Duge Njive-Krajinik," or something else, "Rasevo, Duge Njive, and Glodi were taken and the structures or facilities in Glodi torched. The conditions to execute combat activities are very difficult and visibility is poor." If you're interested in this part of the sentence which mentions the torching of structures in Glodi -- well, I don't know what is of interest to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the part I'm asking about in light of the intercept we saw earlier with General Zivanovic saying, Way to go, about Muslim houses burning. This is now Vinko Pandurevic and Svetozar Andric reporting similar things. What's your view on that in relation to what Mr. Karadzic said about directive 4?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it doesn't say who set the village on fire. Second of all, the village of Glodi was a Serb village. If you know or if you have heard of the plight of Serbs in that village from Glodzansko Brdo, it was done by Oric's soldiers before the new year's 1993. So sometime in December 1992. I do know that our centre for documenting war crimes asked for information from me about the plight of Serbs in Glodzansko Brdo. I don't know the date any more, so I can't see from this document who torched the village. It could have been done by both Serbs and Muslims, but I don't think the Serbs would have torched their own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wasn't there a mosque in Glodi?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that this witness has been able to confirm anything in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Nicholls. We'll not admit this through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. But the witness does know Vinko Pandurevic, does know the date, time, and does know the region, so I think he has impliedly confirmed that, although he didn't recall the exact incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I see the point, but I would like you to tender that document at a later stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. P04253, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is another Vinko Pandurevic document. It may help clear up a question you just posed. It's a supplement to a regular combat report. Please just read the whole thing and tell me when you've read it. Now, the last sentence states -- this is to the Drina Corps command from Vinko Pandurevic, and he states: "We propose that houses should not be torched when taking control of Konjevic Polje, but that they should be inhabited by people from Tuzla and other areas."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And my question is: Can you help us interpret -- what does this last sentence mean, a proposal to the Drina Corps commander not to torch houses in this instance?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's an intelligence proposal, a good proposal. He's asking for the houses not to be torched so that they could be used to accommodate other people. But I don't see why he's making such a proposal. Did someone order him to torch the houses and now he's issuing this order not to torch them? But in any event, the proposal is quite clear here. It says when taking control of Konjevic Polje, the houses should not be torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, in light of the documents we've looked at and the Andric report about burning Gobelji and the intercept we saw about burning Turk houses, let me ask you, why -- why would it be necessary to propose to the command not to burn homes?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Vinko probably had in mind the fact that previously houses had been torched, so now he's requesting that houses shouldn't be torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, the Chamber reconsiders our position regarding 65 ter 21928. Given the content of this document and given the fact that it was drafted at the same time in the Drina Corps area, and the Chamber is of the opinion that witness gave some context to that document, on that basis we'll admit that. Exhibit P4500. I'll ask you to give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 21928 should be assigned Exhibit P4500.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. P2086. This is from the 3rd of March, 1993, a letter from Sadako Ogata to dear Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, unfortunately, I don't think we have a Serbian version, so I'll have to read it to you. 3rd of March, 1993. "United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees" is what it says on the top, General: "Dear Dr. Karadzic, "The reports I receive on the situation in Cerska are appalling. A large number of civilians are blocked in areas which are under military attack. The number of casualties is reportedly high. It is therefore imperative that immediate relief be brought to the victims. "I therefore urge you to authorise UNHCR access, without delay, to the Cerska area. The purpose of UNHCR's intervention will be: "- to bring assistance to the civilian victims; "- to help evacuate the injured; and "- to help evacuate the civilians, especially those who are most vulnerable. "I am counting on your urgent response to this request. "Yours sincerely, Sadako Ogata." And it's address to Dr. Karadzic in Pale. Now this is just in the middle of the Drina Corps and Zvornik Brigade documents we've been looking at. Can you comment on or explain to us if what we've been seeing after directive 4 -- you talked about the Muslim population moving of its own accord, leaving of its own accord, why are these reports reading Dr. Karadzic of an appalling situation for civilians in Cerska?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can this witness say what the reasons are for which Ms. Ogata wrote something of this kind? This is a new examination-in-chief, and I would request that I be granted more time for my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. -- Mr. Karadzic. Yes, General, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm not aware of this letter, the exchange of letter between Mr. Karadzic and Sadako Ogata. I do know who this person is, but I do also know that on the basis of Muslim reports to the international community, General Philippe Morillon, the UNPROFOR commander, went to Cerska, and he stated that the civilian population in Cerska was not abused there. They weren't killed, tortured, and so on and so forth. I assume that Ogata sent him there to see whether those Muslim reports were accurate and she probably sent the letter to Mr. Karadzic before Morillon established what the situation in Cerska actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could I have 65 ter 22824, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a RS Republika Srpska press office communique from the Republika Srpska cabinet of the president, dated 20th of July, 1995, and it states: "President of the republic and the supreme commander of the Srpska armed forces promoted extraordinarily Major-General Milenko Zivanovic, up until recently the commander of the VRS Drina Corps, to the rank of lieutenant-general marking the termination of his active military service. President Karadzic appointed former Chief of Staff, Major-General Radislav Krstic, the commander of the Drina Corps, who, together with General Zivanovic, is the main architect of the Serbian victories in Srebrenica and Zepa. "President Karadzic congratulated the Main Staff of the VRS, the command of the Drina Corps, and the staff of the police armed forces on the brilliant victory in Srebrenica and Zepa as well as crushing the Muslim offends -- offensive in Serbian Sarajevo." On your direct examination with Mr. Karadzic, you said that Zivanovic should not have been a commander. We had the explanation of directive 4 and Zivanovic's order implementing directive 4 which said expressly to force out the Muslim population, and we've seen these documents from when he was command of the Drina Corps in 1992, his subordinates burning villages and him cheering that on. Do you know why he was extraordinarily promoted at the end of his career? I'm just asking if you know the reason.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Was it my duty to comment on this document? And I also shouldn't comment on the decision from the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, didn't you go to a celebration for General Zivanovic's retirement and attend that, and you come all the way from the west to go to that celebration?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I went to that celebration, and I heard about this decree. As far as I am concerned, I don't really know what is in dispute in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, my question is if you knew about this decree and knew about the promotion, if you -- you know, you were -- you were the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff and the deputy commander. If you could tell us why General Zivanovic was promoted rather than possibly being removed or prosecuted for those things we've seen today and yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think that that question is a little bit misleading because the document also indicates that this marks the termination of his active military service, so to -- to characterise this as a promotion without calling the witness's attention to that I think could be misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it is a promotion and I think the witness can read this very well. There is nothing misleading about it, that this was a retirement party, as well, that the general attended. And I called it a retirement celebration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was customary to act in this manner if this was provided for by the law. It was customary to promote someone when retiring so that he could be given an award or something like that and so he could have a better pension. So I don't really see what this has to do with me, what sort of role I had to play with regard to the creation of this document. What does this have to do with the trip to the Han Pijesak restaurant and so on and so forth? What does this have to do with this decree from the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4451, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit number is 4501.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now just let me ask you if -- if you're aware, was -- do you know about General Svetozar Andric also being promoted to become Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps at the same time that Krstic became commander on the 13th of July? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about Andric being appointed as the Chief of Staff of the corps. General Mladic asked me about this, and I was against it. I suggested two other men, General Miletic and Colonel Dragisa Masal. General Mladic said that Miletic was out of the question because he was needed in the Main Staff. He was needed there to be my deputy. And as for Colonel Masal, he dismissed him in advance, saying that when Masal enters Bihac, he should contact him, and he would then be appointed as the Chief of Staff of the corps. I was against Svetozar Andric for the simple reason that this man wasn't up to the task. He couldn't play that role. There were others who were better colonels than he was, and as for me dismissing Andric, that was also because during that period I saw that there was fighting around Srebrenica and Zepa, and I saw Andric with Brada -- I saw Andric with a beard, and I said that the VRS prohibited men from wearing beards apart from in the case of men who wanted to grow a beard for 40 days after the death of a family member. I told Mladic that was the main reason for which I dismissed him, because the colonel had grown a beard as a brigade commander. Mladic laughed, but things remained as he wanted them to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, this document that we're looking at, 20th of July -- yes, 20th of July, 1995, extraordinarily promoting Zivanovic, and Krstic becoming the Drina Corps commander. This is 20th of July. In are view, between the 13th of July, 1995, and the 17th, 18th of July, 1995, how many Muslim prisoners were executed in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm wondering how this arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a huge run-through at the end of the direct that was intended to show that the VRS only waged a defensive war, that the crimes in Sarajevo were committed by the Muslims, that the international community overblew these things and was fooled by it. And essentially the point was that the Serbian side had nothing to do with the start of the war, didn't committed any crimes during the war, and only was defensive in its actions. So I'm simply asking -- this is -- this is an event, it's clear what our case is, that Karadzic did not ask about. I think it's fair to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we're going to open up -- if we're going to open up this area, I hope you give Dr. Karadzic time to re-examine, but I still maintain this is beyond the scope of the direct, the cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can [indiscernible] I'm not the one opening up the area. The area was opened up by the Defence to the suggestion that crimes were not committed by the VRS during the war other than small isolated incidents which they tried to punish through their courts. That was the clear theme of the cross.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say the following: Mr. Nicholls seems to have forgotten that this is a Prosecution witness, and he is saying that I conducted an examination-in-chief. Mr Nicholls had his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was a slip of the tongue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was said on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I meant cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the question. We agree with Mr. Nicholls. Can you answer the question, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't because at the time between the 13th and 19th of July I wasn't in the Main Staff. I was in Drvar and in Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you -- you testified on cross-examination about different things you learned afterwards and what you learned from a lieutenant-colonel about Sarajevo and put in your book, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It wasn't about Srebrenica. Let's move on, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, thank you, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
